lines.L01: Three peaks in one unknown sample. Which compound is which?
lines.L02: GC-MS separates them first, then reads their fragments.
lines.L03: The gas chromatograph: carrier gas, autosampler, heated injector, an oven with a capillary column, and a heated transfer line.
lines.L04: Compounds leave the column at different times: the retention time.
lines.L05: For GC, the analyte must be volatile — sometimes after derivatization.
lines.L06: Then the mass spectrometer: ion source, quadrupole, detector, vacuum pumps and data system.
lines.L07: Molecules are ionised and break into fragment ions.
lines.L08: The quadrupole sorts ions by mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, and passes them in turn.
lines.L09: The result: a chromatogram over retention time, and a mass spectrum for every peak.
lines.L10: Compounds are identified against a spectral library or standards.
lines.L11: Without quality control, peaks that don’t belong to the sample can appear.
lines.L12: In LabGuide: Lab → Instruments and methods → Toxicology → the GC-MS card.
lines.L13: The same schematic and parts, then principle and tasks — each sourced.
lines.L14: QC notes and biosafety are on the card too: hot parts, glasses, coat and gloves.
lines.L15: From peak to identity — one step at a time.
lines.L16: LabGuide — Lab → Instruments and methods → GC-MS.
